title: What Impacts the strength of perceived barriers to and drivers of energy efficiency in manufacturing SMEs?

# What Impacts the strength of perceived barriers to and drivers of energy efficiency in manufacturing SMEs?

PMC10806267. Heliyon, 10(1):e24020. Published 2024-01-05.

## Authors

Janez Dolšak, Nevenka Hrovatin, Jelena Zorić

## Details

- DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e24020
- PMID: 38268578 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38268578/)
- PMCID: PMC10806267
- License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/

---

## Abstract

In the manufacturing sector, improving energy efficiency in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) is typically more challenging than in larger companies. Although the barriers to and drivers of energy efficiency measures (EEMs) are relatively well researched and identified in the literature, little attention has been paid to the factors that influence how SMEs perceive them. This study uses a sample of 220 manufacturing SMEs in Slovenia to econometrically assess the relevance of a comprehensive set of firm-, business-, energy- and energy efficiency–related characteristics to the barriers to and drivers of EEMs identified in the literature. The objective of this study is to identify which factors influence the importance of various barriers and drivers while accounting for firm heterogeneity. The results show that among the most influential factors of perceived barriers are energy intensity and export orientation, which are associated with the lower importance of perceived barriers, while debt works in the opposite direction. Surprisingly, firm size does not have an impact on barriers, except for one – the additional risk involved in EE investments, whereas it impacts several drivers. A low level of competition in the market and ownership of the firm's premises also contribute to the lower intensity of perceived barriers. In terms of the perceived importance of drivers, the most influential factors are firm size, the presence of an energy-responsible person in the firm and the company's employee energy efficiency awareness programme. Among the approaches to improve energy efficiency, the introduction of an energy policy or energy management system and certifications have the greatest influence on removing barriers, while energy consulting is not found to be significant. Furthermore, the importance of drivers is mainly positively associated with energy audits. These results provide useful policy implications for how to address the energy efficiency gap in manufacturing SMEs by targeting factors that would most effectively lower barriers to and strengthen drivers of energy efficiency.

• Determinants of the barriers and drivers of EEMs are studied. • Examining a large set of determinants with discrete choice models. • A representative sample of 220 manufacturing SMEs. • Barriers are related to energy intensity, export orientation, and indebtedness. • Drivers are related to size, importance of EE in the company, and energy audit.

## Introduction

Industrial energy efficiency (EE) is of paramount importance for achieving the energy policies and development goals of EU member states. It offers significant potential to enhance competitiveness, promote green growth and generate employment opportunities. EE plays a crucial role in ensuring the strategic security of supply by reducing the reliance on fossil fuel imports and encouraging sustainable energy resource use. It is also a cost-effective approach to curbing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and increasing the proportion of renewable energy sources (RES) in the final energy consumption balance. Across Europe, several policy measures are available to enhance EE, such as subsidies, soft loans, pricing instruments, efficiency standards and research and development (R&D) grants for energy-efficient technologies and materials. These measures are often accompanied by various awareness programmes and training initiatives aimed at improving EE, including product labelling, professional training and awareness campaigns. However, the factors that influence the perceived barriers to and drivers of EE in companies, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), have not been extensively studied. Cost-effective energy efficiency measures (EEMs) are among the approaches aimed at improving EE, but their utilisation is low, which gives rise to the so-called energy efficiency gap [[1], [2], [3]]. Closing this gap could pose a more substantial challenge for SMEs in the manufacturing sector given their constrained financial resources and limited access to energy professionals. However, their inherent business agility and flexibility can be harnessed to expedite their adoption of EEMs.

The successful implementation of any policy will depend not only on knowing which barriers to and drivers of cost-efficient EEMs are present in the firm but also understanding the determinants of barriers that impede the adoption of EEMs or the determinants of drivers that encourage their adoption, as this will aid in designing the most effective approaches [2,4,5]. Presumably, firms are heterogeneous in their perceptions of the barriers to and drivers of EEMs. This could be because of differences in firm- and business-related characteristics as well as energy- and EE-related characteristics. Several authors have identified differences between firms that could influence their perceptions of barriers to and drivers of EEMs. For example, Schleich [5] found that EE is a more important issue in energy-intensive than in non-energy-intensive firms. In particular, EE rarely plays an important role in SMEs, because these companies typically have few resources for energy management [6,7]. Typical barriers in these companies relate to transaction and hidden costs and a lack of information, which mainly affect non-energy-intensive companies with relatively low knowledge of the energy processes in the company.

Empirical analyses of the determinants of barriers of and drivers to EEMs in SMEs are very scarce, and existing studies have tended to use a case study approach rather than an econometric approach, which would require a large sample of firms, which is often difficult to obtain (e.g. Refs. [[8], [9], [10]]). In most cases, these works describe the relevance of barriers to and/or drivers of EE (e.g. Refs. [11,12]). In some cases, the determinants of such barriers and drivers have been analysed using multivariate regression models (e.g. Refs. [4,5,13,14]). However, these analyses have typically considered firms as a homogeneous group and have not accounted for potential differences across firms. Only Schleich [15] and de Groot et al. [16] used the econometric approach to examine which determinants influence firms’ perceptions of barriers to and drivers of EEMs, while other studies addressed this question indirectly (e.g. Ref. [17]). Most studies found that various firm and market characteristics matter for EEM adoption, and we hypothesise that these characteristics also matter for perceptions of barriers and drivers, and these perceptions may discourage or motivate firms to invest.

The research setting of this paper is Slovenia, which is following the EU Energy Strategy with the ambitious goal of increasing EE by at least 32.5 % by 2030 compared to the base year 2007 [18]. In 2020, Slovenia adopted the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) and set key strategic targets, including increasing EE by at least 35 % compared to the 2007 baseline [19]. According to the NECP, the goals for supporting SMEs focus on developing a system for promoting EEMs in SMEs, especially on removing the barriers to their implementation. SMEs are also a priority area of the EU policy action for transformative change in the recently adopted package of legislative proposals, Fit for 55 [20]. With this strategy, the European Commission aims to achieve climate neutrality by 2050, with net emissions reduced by at least 55 % by 2030 compared to 1990 levels. SMEs have been identified as particularly vulnerable and as having fewer resources and information to ensure a successful green transition. In summary, SMEs will be one of the main targets of Slovenian and EU EE policies in the near future.

Despite the successful achievement of national EE targets in 2014–2016, as assessed by the European Commission [21], recent achievements in Slovenian industrial EE have been modest. In particular, annual industrial energy savings fell by 37.1 % over the period 2016–2019 [22]. The annual report of Eco Fund, the main provider of financial support for Slovenian companies to increase EE, reveals that in 2019, only 10 % of all Eco Fund loans were granted to these companies, compared to 23 % in 2018 and 40 % in 2017 [23]. By contrast, the final energy consumption for manufacturing and construction increased by 14.6 % in 2019 compared to 2016, while the gross value added in these sectors increased by only 13.1 % over the same period [24]. This corresponds to a 28.6 % share of final energy in the country, which is five percentage points more than in 2017. For its energy needs, industry mainly uses electricity (41.8 %), while renewable energy sources and natural gas account for 10.3 % and 8.6 %, respectively [25]. Thus, due to the significant increase in its energy consumption, industry contributed only 23 % to the cumulative energy savings in the period 2012–2020 [19]. Reversing the growing trend in energy consumption of industry and its role in achieving the planned EE level by 2030 is crucial.

This study utilises econometric methods to evaluate the impact of various factors on the barriers to and drivers of EE. A total of 220 Slovenian manufacturing SMEs surveyed in 2019 are analysed. We draw from two mentioned econometric studies investigating the determinants of barriers to EE – namely, those by Schleich [15] and de Groot et al. [16]. These sources provide valuable insights into the intricate interactions between various variables within our research context. By considering the evidence presented in these works, we approach our analysis with a nuanced understanding of the interplay between different factors. While the studies on which we rely focus on examining barriers, we have additionally included a comprehensive set of drivers and expanded the range of explanatory variables by incorporating not only several company characteristics but also a large set of variables specifically related to energy and EE within a company. Each barrier and driver is examined separately with the same set of explanatory variables in each regression.

The purpose of this paper is to identify the factors influencing the perceived barriers to and drivers of EEMs among Slovenian manufacturing SMEs and examine the impact of heterogeneity among companies to determine which of the two groups of explanatory variables (firm- and business-related and energy- and EE-related characteristics) has a greater influence on the perceived barriers to and drivers of EEMs using the selected models. The outcomes of this research can be utilised to assess the effectiveness of current industrial EE policies in Slovenia and offer deeper insights into the determinants of barriers to and drivers of EE.

The study makes three significant contributions to knowledge. First, it provides new insights into the factors that impact firms’ perceptions of barriers to and drivers of adopting energy-efficient measures using data from a representative sample of 10 % of Slovenian SMEs in the manufacturing sector, enabling the results to be generalised to the entire sector. Second, the study examines the potential effects of a comprehensive set of factors on both the perceived barriers to and drivers of adopting cost-effective EEMs. Lastly, the study explores in depth a broad range of factors related to energy and EE, thereby uncovering new dimensions of the EE gap.
